analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from ever lobbying and extends staff lobbying bans to six years.
analysis.headline: The Close the Revolving Door Act never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have imposed a lifetime lobbying ban on former senators, representatives, and elected congressional officers, replacing the current two-year ban for senators and one-year ban for House members. It would have stretched the ban on senior congressional staff from one year to six, barred registered lobbyists who had substantial contact with a member or committee from being hired by that office for six years, forced large lobbying firms to disclose the former lawmakers and senior staff they hire as consultants, and raised the maximum penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000. It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary citizens would have gained a Congress less staffed by people whose careers run through the lobbying industry, and congressional offices would have been less likely to write laws with their next employers in mind. Current members and staff would face clearer rules about the line between public service and cashing in on it. The public would also have gotten a single searchable website, lobbyists.gov, showing who is lobbying whom and which firms employ former lawmakers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, and congressional offices seeking independence

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a lifetime ban on former senators, House members, and elected congressional officers from lobbying Congress, replacing the current two-year ban for ex-senators and one-year ban for ex-representatives.
Extends the lobbying ban for Senate officers, personal, committee, and leadership staff, and other legislative offices from one year to six years after they leave.

Bars any registered lobbyist or foreign-agent registrant from being hired by a member or committee they lobbied substantially for six years, with contacts on pending legislation, earmarks, meetings, or fundraising counting toward 'substantial contact'.

Requires any incorporated firm employing more than three registered lobbyists to file an annual public list of the former members of Congress and senior or highly paid legislative branch officials it employs or pays as consultants, with job descriptions, and to send copies to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to check for underreported lobbying.

Creates a single searchable public database, lobbyists.gov, run by the Secretary of the Senate and Clerk of the House, and raises the civil penalty ceiling for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and the growing industry that turns former lawmakers and senior staff into paid influencers would bear the cost: ex-members would lose the most lucrative use of their connections, and firms could no longer hire a staffer one year and deploy them against their old boss the next. Congressional offices would face a smaller hiring pool, since experienced registered lobbyists could not join an office they had lobbied for six years. Taxpayers would fund the small cost of the new disclosure website, authorized at $100,000.

drawbacks.text: The lobbyist-hiring ban contains a built-in escape valve: the Senate Ethics Committee or the House ethics committee can waive it for any individual based on a 'compelling national need', leaving room for case-by-case exceptions.

The new consultant-disclosure rule only covers firms with more than three registered lobbyists, so smaller shops — and any arrangement where a former member is paid as a 'consultant' rather than a registered lobbyist — could stay off the public list, which is why the bill pairs disclosure with Justice Department review rather than closing the gap outright.

Stretching the staff ban from one year to six years makes congressional work a longer detour from a private-sector career, which could make it harder for offices to recruit experienced people — a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh against the benefit of staff not cashing in on their old committees.

A lifetime ban on former members lobbying reaches conduct long after they leave office, and enforcement would depend entirely on Justice Department prosecutions under criminal penalty provisions; a restriction this long-running could face First Amendment challenges about the government restricting petitioning activity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core restrictions — a lifetime ban for ex-members and six-year bans for staff and for offices hiring the lobbyists who targeted them — would meaningfully cut the fastest route by which policy access is sold, and the disclosure-plus-prosecution design shows the drafters understood the consulting workaround. But the bill is not airtight: the ethics-committee waiver, the three-lobbyist threshold that exempts smaller firms, and the fact that disclosure of consultants is not the same as barring them all leave avenues open. The main cost is a thinner talent pipeline for congressional offices. On balance the benefits to the public outweigh those costs, which is part of why the lobbying industry's quiet interest in its disappearance matters.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on July 27, 2023, with Senator Michael Bennet, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote appear in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 118th Congress.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats, and died on January 3, 2025, when the 118th Congress ended and all unpassed bills expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and former members of Congress who sell their access came out ahead: the current rules — one to two years out of office before lobbying — remain in place, and the disclosure and penalty provisions that would have shined light on the consulting side of the industry were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbying firms and ex-lawmakers cashing in

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from sponsorship: the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have stretched cooling-off periods to six years and, for former members, forever, shrinking the pool of connected hires firms can offer clients and raising the penalty ceiling for disclosure violations to $500,000. Because the bill never advanced, the industry's current one-to-two-year revolving door remains intact.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress monetizing their access
industries.note: A lifetime lobbying ban plus mandatory annual disclosure of any firm paying an ex-member as a consultant would have ended the standard post-Congress career path of selling relationships on K Street. The bill's death preserves that market.

Firms with more than three registered lobbyists would have had to publicly list every former lawmaker and senior staffer they pay as a consultant, with the filings sent to the D.C. U.S. Attorney to check for underreporting. Firms below that threshold, or individuals who avoid registering at all, would have escaped the new reporting — a gap the bill acknowledged but did not close.
